paper_title: Noise Out, Bias In: Targeted Bias Injection in Diffusion Language Models via Closed-Loop Activation Steering

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Masked diffusion language models (dLLMs) generate text by iteratively denoising masked positions, re-predicting each token multiple times before it is committed. An autoregressive decoder exposes an answer's distribution once, at the step that commits it; a dLLM exposes it at every denoising step before commitment, and we show that an adversary can exploit this. Since an answer remains open to revision over many denoising steps, an adversary with access to internal activations can watch how likely the model is to produce a chosen answer and adjust the intervention accordingly. Building on this observation, we study targeted bias injection, an attack that steers a frozen dLLM toward a demographic answer selected by the adversary. The attack uses a simple proportional-integral (PI) controller that tracks the target-answer probability during denoising and adapts the strength of a steering vector on the fly. On ambiguous BBQ questions where the correct answer is abstention, our attack raises LLaDA-8B-Instruct's preference for the targeted group from 1.8 to 16.7 percentage points, more than three times the strongest fixed-strength steering baseline, and on SocialStigmaQA it raises the selection of stigmatizing answers from 17.6% to 58.1%. Fitted to other demographic targets, the same attack shifts answers by up to 37 percentage points, and each attack takes about 40 minutes on one GPU. On the primary target, feedback is what makes the attack work: constant steering at the same average strength over the token-committing steps produces a far smaller shift while corrupting nearly three times as many outputs, and a constant strength set separately for each example still falls well short. Our findings identify the denoising trajectory as a new control channel in dLLMs and call for bias audits that examine the serving stack rather than the frozen model alone.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) generate text by iteratively denoising masked sequence instead of predicting one token after another (Li et al., 2022; Austin et al., 2021; Lou et al., 2024; Sahoo et al., 2024). Open models such as LLaDA (Nie et al., 2025), Dream (Ye et al., 2025), and LLaDA-MoE (Zhu et al., 2025) now match autoregressive models of similar scale, which makes them candidates for the same uses, from customer-facing assistants (Brynjolfsson et al., 2025) to hiring and other screening decisions (Burema et al., 2026). Because they are trained on similar corpora and instruction-tuned in similar ways (Ouyang et al., 2022), there is no reason to expect them to be any fairer. Autoregressive LLMs carry stereotypes from their training data into their answers (Thaler et al., 2026; Nadeem et al., 2021; Li et al., 2020; Parrish et al., 2022), in free generation (Wan & Chang, 2025; Pan et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026) as much as in question answering (Jin et al., 2025) and across languages (Mitchell et al., 2025; Saeed et al., 2026; Gamboa et al., 2025), and alignment

Shading marks steps after the last token commits. removes explicit bias more reliably than the implicit associations behind it (Bai et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2025b). The same pattern has already been seen in dLLMs. On an income-prediction task, TrustLDM (Mo et al., 2026) finds gender disparities in both LLaDA and Dream, and malicious context makes them worse. Audits of this kind measure the bias that training leaves in models weights. Bias can also be added later, at inference time, by whoever controls the models inputs or its serving stack. For autoregressive LLMs, crafted prompts can pull answers toward chosen demographic group (Zhao et al., 2025a), and so can steering vector added to the residual stream (Wang & Shu, 2024). The second route goes through the same forward hooks that activation steering (Turner et al., 2023; Rimsky et al., 2024; Li et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2023; Arditi et al., 2024; Rodríguez et al., 2025; Suau et al., 2024) uses for benign control and FairSteer (Li et al., 2025) uses for debiasing, and it leaves the weights and the users prompt exactly as they were, so an audit of the checkpoint or of the prompt pipeline finds nothing. Whether deployed system is biased therefore depends on its serving stack as well as its checkpoint, and for dLLMs that stack has not been examined at all. Examining it is not matter of directly using the autoregressive attack, because the two decoders give an attacker different information. Nguyen et al. (2026) have shown that activation steering is control problem. Here the output is the probability of the target answer at the unresolved position, and the input is the steering strength α. An autoregressive model exposes that probability only when it commits the token, so α has to be chosen before generation, and the steering methods proposed so far for dLLMs (Shnaidman et al., 2026; Avrahami & Nachmani, 2026; Zhou et al., 2026) keep this openloop form. Open-loop control presumes known response, and here there is none. How far given α moves the answer depends on the examples initial leaning toward the target and on its sensitivity to the direction, and neither is visible until the intervention is applied. single α is therefore too small for the resistant examples or large enough to break the output of the others, and even an α chosen separately for each example in advance falls well short of feedback. masked dLLM removes the constraint behind open-loop control. It re-predicts the unresolved answer position at every denoising step until it commits, so the target probability can be measured after each intervention and the next α chosen from it. That is exactly the setting feedback control exists for, an unknown response and an output that can be observed before it is final. The controller pushes where the answer resists and eases off as it approaches the setpoint (see Figure 1), and with integral action it converges to the α each example needs (Section 3). This paper studies that attack, which we call targeted bias injection. An adversary with gray-box access to deployed dLLMs residual stream steers its answers to ambiguous questions, whose correct answer is abstention, toward demographic group of its choice and away from the questions other demographic option, the comparator (see Figure 2). We fit one direction offline and let proportionalintegral (PI) controller set its strength during denoising from the target-answer probability; direction, injection sites, weights, and prompt stay fixed. We evaluate on ambiguous questions from BBQ (Parrish et al., 2022) and on three-option version of SocialStigmaQA (Nagireddy et al., 2024), scoring the change in the targetcomparator gap relative to the unsteered model.

(a) Schematic of the attack: the frozen model is steered along fixed direction, and after each denoising pass the attacker reads the target-answer probability at the unresolved answer position and adjusts the strength for the next pass; locks mark token commitment. Our experiments ask how much bias the attack injects, whether feedback rather than fixed strength is what makes it work, whether it transfers across targets, benchmarks, and models, and whether the same loop can serve as defense (Section 4). Our contributions are: 1. We identify the denoising trajectory of dLLMs as feedback channel for inference-time attacks and introduce closed-loop targeted bias injection, decode-time PI controller that adapts the strength of one fixed steering direction from the target-answer probability, leaving weights and prompts untouched. 2. On LLaDA-8B-Instruct the attack raises the BBQ targetcomparator gap by 14.9 (Black), 22.5 (Arab), and 37.2 (Old) percentage points and lifts stigmatizing answers on SocialStigmaQA from 17.6% to 58.1%, with no training and about 40 minutes on one GPU per target. 3. With control-theoretic model of the loop and effort-matched open loops across three dLLMs and seven steering baselines, we show that feedback wins exactly when no single strength serves every example, and that tuned constant does better.

sections.title: 2 THREAT MODEL
sections.content: Adversary knowledge and objective. provider deploys frozen dLLM behind an API. The adversary controls compromised component of the serving stack that can register forward hooks on the residual stream at inference, the same interface prior work uses to plant trojaned steering vectors in autoregressive LLMs (Wang & Shu, 2024). Forward hooks are the standard interface of steering and interpretability libraries (Zou et al., 2023; Rimsky et al., 2024), and they act below the text interface, leaving weights, prompts, and the sampler unchanged, so an audit of the checkpoint or of the prompt pipeline finds nothing to flag. Attacks through the prompt (Zhao et al., 2025a; Wen et al., 2026) or the decoding procedure (Zhang et al., 2025), and direct edits to logits or responses, lie outside this interface. Access is gray-box. The adversary reads residual activations, adds bounded offsets through the hooks, and observes the intermediate answer-token probabilities that the sampler already computes for remasking (Nie et al., 2025), but it cannot inspect weights, compute gradients, or train. On ambiguous questions whose correct answer is abstention (Parrish et al., 2022), the adversary wants the model to select designated protected-group option instead. Over the position-balanced item distribution, we score the attack by the expected margin between selecting the target and the comparator, = E(cid:2)1{pick = target} 1{pick = comparator}(cid:3), (1) the targetcomparator gap of Section 4. successful attack drives well above the unsteered gap while keeping outputs coherent, so we report the invalid-output rate alongside every gap; all runs fit in one GPU hour per target (Appendix B).

sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: Our experiments address four questions: 1) how much targeted bias closed-loop steering can inject into frozen dLLM, and how it compares with existing activation-steering methods (Section 4.2); 2) whether the gain is due to feedback itself rather than to the steering direction, the injection sites, or strength chosen once per example (Section 4.3); 3) whether the attack transfers to other demographic targets, to second benchmark, and to other dLLMs (Section 4.4); and 4) whether the same loop can be run in reverse as defense, and how much evaluation choices change the measured effect (Section 4.5). Section 4.1 describes the setup. 4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP Models. LLaDA-8B-Instruct (Nie et al., 2025) is the primary model, run frozen with 32-token single-block generation, 64 denoising steps, temperature 0, and low-confidence remasking; Dreamv0-Instruct-7B (Ye et al., 2025) and LLaDA-MoE-7B-A1B-Instruct (Zhu et al., 2025) test transfer (Appendix B). Datasets. The primary task is 400 ambiguous Black-target questions from BBQ (Parrish et al., 2022), where abstention is correct and the other demographic option is the comparator, each shown under three rotations of its answer options (1,200 prompts). Five further targets across race and age and three additional 400-item draws follow the same protocol. Metrics. strict parser accepts response only if it begins with an answer letter, and invalid outputs stay in every denominator. We report target, comparator, abstention, and invalid rates, the gap of Equation 1, and its change from the unsteered model, g, in percentage points; green cells shift answers toward the target and red cells away. Intervals are 95% paired bootstraps over prompts for BBQ and over templates for SocialStigmaQA, and item-clustered intervals leave every comparison unchanged in sign (Appendix A.3, Figure 4). 4.2 RQ1: HOW MUCH BIAS CAN BE INJECTED? Table 1 reports the primary evaluation. Closed-loop steering lifts the targetcomparator gap from 1.8 to 16.7, while no baseline exceeds 4.6, and the 95% intervals of the three decode-time rows lie entirely above those of every baseline, whether prompts or items are resampled (Figures 6 and 4). The result does not rest on the calibration items. Removing the 100 items used to fix the gains leaves gap of 16.2 on the other 300, with PI still ahead of every baseline by at least 12.1, and three further item draws give mean gap of 16.2 against 0.3 for the unsteered model (Appendix C.4). The attack has cost in coherence, which the tables never hide: 7.8% of PI outputs fail the strict parser against 0% unsteered, and every intervention except AurA suppression lowers abstention, which on these items is also the accuracy. 4.3 RQ2: IS FEEDBACK RESPONSIBLE FOR THE GAIN? The ablations in Table 1 share the direction and injection sites with the controller and differ only in how the strength is set. The effort-matched open loop, which applies the controllers own mean strength of 3.28 as constant, reaches gap of only 3.5 while corrupting 20.8% of outputs, against 7.8% under feedback. This is Proposition 1 in practice, one strength that is too weak for some items and too strong for others. Choosing the constant per item does not close the gap either. strength set from the unsteered probe p0 reaches 4.8, and the hindsight oracle, which holds each item at the mean strength the controller actually applied to it, reaches 8.4 at the same overall mean of 3.28. PI leads the oracle by 8.3 points, difference whose interval excludes zero (Figure 4), with fewer invalid outputs (7.8% against 13.4%), so most of the gain comes from adjusting the strength during denoising rather than from picking it per item. Figure 1 shows the mechanism at work. The controller raises the strength on items that resist and lowers it once the target probability nears the setpoint, and 78% of sequences reduce their command at least once in response to the measurement (Appendix C.7). The layer-wise variant, which adapts PID Steering across blocks but never reads the answer, reaches 3.1. 4.4 RQ3: DOES THE ATTACK TRANSFER? Table 3 summarizes the other targets and models; full method grids and intervals are in Appendix C. On LLaDA-8B, Arab is the strongest race target that stays below 15% invalidity, at gap of 22.3, and Old gives the largest shift overall, = 37.2; on both, the effort-matched open loop again trails feedback (Appendix C.2). PI exceeds the invalidity threshold on Asian, Latino, and White, and we report those runs as failures rather than attacks (Appendix C).

sections.title: 5 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Activation steering edits frozen models hidden states at inference time along directions built from prompt pairs (Turner et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2023), averaged contrasts (Rimsky et al., 2024), head-level edits (Li et al., 2023), neuron damping (Suau et al., 2024), or transport maps (Rodríguez et al., 2025), and it has been used both to reduce bias (Li et al., 2025) and to plant it, in the Trojan activation attack (Wang & Shu, 2024) that our threat model follows. PID Steering reads layer-wise steering as proportional controller and adds integral and derivative terms across depth (Nguyen et al., 2026), whereas our loop runs across denoising steps with the attackers answer probability as the measured output. Steering of masked diffusion models so far fixes the intervention before generation (Shnaidman et al., 2026; Avrahami & Nachmani, 2026; Zhou et al., 2026), and attacks on dLLMs seek harmful compliance through the prompt (Wen et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2026; He et al., 2026), the decoding procedure (Zhang et al., 2025; Singh, 2026), or safety neurons (Dumitrescu et al., 2026), with DiffuGuard as the corresponding defense (Li et al., 2026) and TrustLDM as the first bias audit (Mo et al., 2026); we instead induce targeted demographic preference through activations. Our benchmarks come from the bias-measurement literature (Li et al., 2020; Parrish et al., 2022; Nagireddy et al., 2024), whose sensitivity to answer position, parsing, and abstention our protocol controls for. Appendix gives fuller account.

sections.title: 6 DISCUSSION
sections.content: Conclusion. masked dLLM re-predicts an answer many times before committing it, and this paper shows that an adversary with hooks on the residual stream can use those predictions as feedback signal. PI controller that reads the target-answer probability and adjusts one steering direction during denoising shifts frozen dLLMs answers toward the attackers group by several times what the best fixed-strength baseline achieves, on BBQ and on SocialStigmaQA, without touching weights or prompts. The ablations locate the gain in feedback itself. constant matched to the controllers mean strength moves the gap little while breaking far more outputs, and even per-example constant chosen with hindsight recovers under half of the effect. The theory says when to expect this. Feedback pays where the strength an example needs varies widely, as on Black-target BBQ and SocialStigmaQA, and adds little where one strength serves every item; LLaDA-MoE, where tuned constant wins, and Dream, where the coherent bound pins the controller, mark the two ends of that range. Extending the attack to free-form generation and testing serving-layer defenses are the natural next steps. The broader point is that models bias is property of the deployed system, and audits that stop at the checkpoint will miss it. Implications for auditing and defense. checkpoint audit passes model whose deployment is biased. Audits should probe the served endpoint, and this attack leaves cheap signature there, since it lowers abstention on ambiguous questions and raises invalid outputs, both visible on fixed probe set without knowing the target group. Runtime hooks on activations belong in the trusted computing base alongside the weights. The same loop with zero setpoint acts as suppressor, but we have tested it only where the unsteered gap is already near zero. Limitations. Controller gains were chosen on 100 of the 400 primary items, and although removing them changes no comparison in sign, several per-target strengths were also selected on evaluation data. We study multiple-choice answers read from letter probability; free-form generation, where the target has no single token to measure, is untested, and the SocialStigmaQA result shows transfer

sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: Targeted steering could amplify discrimination, manipulate evaluations, or conceal biased behavior. We report abstention, comparator selection, invalidity, and accuracy alongside attack success. Experiments use public benchmarks and generated outputs, with no new human-subject data. Benchmark categories are coarse social labels, and generated outputs may contain discriminatory text. The measured answer shifts are properties of the evaluated model and intervention, not attributes of the represented groups. These experiments do not establish deployable bias-mitigation method.

sections.title: REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT
sections.content: Our code implements direction fitting, generation, intervention, rotation, and evaluation; Equations 3 6 specify the direction, interventions, and controllers. Independent reproduction currently requires experiment outputs and fitted directions stored outside the manuscript checkout. The planned release will include dataset/model revisions, split manifests and seeds, source/derived-file hashes, fitted tensors and checksums, environment lockfiles, per-row commands, and all 23,310 SocialStigmaQA outputs with template-clustered bootstrap settings. Planned packaging work includes replacing absolute paths, rejecting missing directions, logging hook attachment, and regenerating tables in clean worktree from immutable outputs using shared strict parsing and metrics that retain invalid responses. The table-generation scripts will ship with the artifact. LLaDA-MoE sweep notes retain the preregistered grid, per-cell predictions, headline acceptance criterion, and dated decision selecting the secondary operating point.

sections.content: The conventions in this appendix apply to every BBQ result unless table states otherwise. SocialStigmaQA follows the same conventions and additionally reports semantic parser and gap conditioned on valid outputs (Appendix C.8). A.1 ANSWER PARSING AND SCORING response is valid only when an answer letter, in either case, begins the response and is followed by whitespace, punctuation, or the end of the string; every other response is strict-invalid. This rule replaces legacy parser that accepted the first A, B, or character anywhere in free text and thereby turned malformed prose into answers. Invalid responses stay in the denominator of every rate. Target and comparator rates are fractions of all evaluated prompts, the gap is the target rate minus the comparator rate, and is conditions gap minus the unsteered gap on the same target. sections.title: E EXTENDED RELATED WORK
sections.content: This appendix expands the related-work summary of Section 5. E.1 ACTIVATION STEERING AND ITS CONTROL-THEORETIC READING Activation interventions edit frozen models hidden states at inference time, using directions built from prompt pairs (Turner et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2023), averaged contrasts (Rimsky et al., 2024), head-level edits (Li et al., 2023), neuron damping (Suau et al., 2024), or optimal-transport maps (Rodríguez et al., 2025); single direction can carry behavior such as refusal (Arditi et al., 2024). FairSteer applies debiasing direction only when probe on the activations detects bias (Li et al., 2025); the Trojan activation attack plants direction to induce misaligned outputs (Wang & Shu, 2024), the autoregressive precedent for our threat model. PID Steering reads the layer-wise construction of steering vector as proportional controller and adds integral and derivative terms across network depth (Nguyen et al., 2026). Our loop runs along different axis: the same network at successive denoising steps, with the probability of the attackers answer as the measured output and single scalar strength under control.

sections.content: E.2 INFERENCE-TIME CONTROL AND ATTACKS ON DLLMS Shnaidman et al. (2026) suppress refusal by removing activation components along fixed direction throughout reverse diffusion, Avrahami & Nachmani (2026) align representations with reference sequence at each step, and Zhou et al. (2026) schedule interventions by when attributes emerge; none uses the evolving probability of designated answer as feedback. Adversarial work on dLLMs seeks harmful compliance: DIJA interleaves masked spans with harmful prompts so that bidirectional infilling completes them (Wen et al., 2026), MaskForge automates the search over such structures (Ma et al., 2026), PAD steers parallel decoding toward affirmative continuations (Zhang et al., 2025), He et al. (2026) nest harmful requests in benign context, Singh (2026) re-mask committed refusal tokens, and Dumitrescu et al. (2026) prune safety-related neurons; DiffuGuard defends the denoising loop against such attacks (Li et al., 2026). TrustLDM audits dLLMs for bias and shows that malicious context amplifies it (Mo et al., 2026). We instead induce targeted demographic preference through activations, without touching the prompt, weights, or commitment schedule. E.3 MEASURING DEMOGRAPHIC BIAS Underspecified questions expose reliance on stereotypes when abstention is the correct answer (Li et al., 2020; Parrish et al., 2022), and SocialStigmaQA tests whether generation amplifies documented stigmas (Nagireddy et al., 2024); broader benchmarks cover stereotypes in pretrained models and in generated text (Nadeem et al., 2021; Jin et al., 2025; Wan & Chang, 2025). We repurpose BBQ and SocialStigmaQA as attack objectives and inherit their pitfalls: answer position, abstention handling, invalid generations, and response parsing all change the apparent effect, and Section 4 controls for each.
